t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we will learn to analyse an unknown object and to draw up an expert report. The aim is to familiarise students with forensic chemical examination, its specific features, the plan of a chemical-toxicological investigation and the duties of expert chemists. The plan has two items. First, the report of a forensic chemical investigation. Second, chemical-toxicological examination.

As a result of the session, students will gain knowledge of forensic chemical examination, its bureau and its staff. They will also learn about the forensic chemical investigation report and about chemical-toxicological examination. Required items: extract, filter paper, funnel, reagents, test tubes, visual aids, adhesive tape and paper. The work is carried out in a room equipped with special laboratory apparatus.

Safety rules. The student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask to the laboratory work. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard. After the work such rooms are locked and sealed. Objects from persons with infectious diseases, that is tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, arrive in a special container and are marked in the documents.

t: Why is forensic chemical examination carried out?
n: Why is forensic chemical examination carried out? It is carried out to establish the presence, nature and quantity of poisonous substances that harm health or lead to death. The examination also helps medical workers to improve medical care for the population and to prevent poisoning. It may be carried out in order to give urgent medical care to a poisoned person, or on the written instruction of investigating bodies or a hospital.

The forensic chemical investigation report consists of 4 parts: the introductory part, the external appearance of the physical evidence, the chemical investigation and the expert's conclusion. The introductory part states the basis document, the laboratory, the expert, the victim and the time of the investigation. The external appearance part records the wrapping, container, seal, colour, odour, weight and the pH of the medium. The chemical investigation is the main part of the report and is set out in sequence on the basis of the entries in the working notebook. In the conclusion, the poisons found are given in mg per 100 g of material.

t: Documents and object received for examination
n: Documents and object received for examination. The laboratory is sent the written ruling ordering the examination, an extract from the forensic medical report and an extract from the case history. The physical evidence is sent through the institution and entered in the laboratory's registration log; if the wrapping has been damaged, a report is drawn up. The expert is responsible for keeping the evidence from the start of the investigation to its end and works according to a plan he or she has drawn up. If the ruling does not state which poisons to test for, the object is tested for the poisons approved by the Ministry of Health.

Laboratory logs. Three logs are kept in forensic chemical laboratories. The first is the registration log, which has 16 sections. The second is the forensic chemist's working notebook, in which daily calculations are recorded. The third is the report book, in which the handwritten report is kept and sealed. The working notebook and the report book are numbered, bound with cord and sealed.

Organic poisons: 28 substances. In a complete chemical-toxicological analysis, 28 organic poisons are tested for. They fall into three groups: 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds.

t: List of organic poisons: the numbers
n: Let us repeat the list of organic poisons with the numbers. In a complete chemical-toxicological analysis, 28 substances are tested for. They include 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds. Remember: the largest number of substances is in the alkaloid group, namely 14.

t: List of substances to be tested
n: List of substances to be tested. Barbiturates: barbital, phenobarbital, barbamyl, etaminal sodium, cyclobarbital, that is phenodorm, hexobarbital, that is evipan, and benzonal. Alkaloids: morphine, codeine, dionine, heroin, hydrocodone, papaverine, strychnine, atropine, that is hyoscyamine, scopolamine, cocaine, pachycarpine, anabasine, nicotine and quinine. Nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds: promedol, aminazine, diprazine, tizercin, mazheptil, triftazin, imizine and its analogues.

t: Groups of organic poisons and examples
n: Let us briefly recall the groups and examples. Barbiturates: barbital, phenobarbital, barbamyl, etaminal sodium, cyclobarbital, hexobarbital, benzonal. Nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds: promedol, aminazine, diprazine, tizercin, mazheptil, triftazin, imizine. Alkaloids: morphine, codeine, strychnine, atropine, scopolamine, cocaine, nicotine, quinine and others. There are 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 nitrogen-containing synthetics.

Isolation methods using polar solvents. The substances above are mainly crystalline medicinal substances; they are isolated from the object with acidified water and acidified alcohol. Under acidic conditions, barbiturates and alkaloids form salts through the nitrogen atom and pass into the aqueous or alcoholic solution. The aqueous solution is extracted with organic solvents, because the substances may have acidic, basic or neutral properties.

The Stas-Otto method. This method was proposed by J.S. Stas in 1851; in 1856 F. Otto added purification of the alcoholic extract. The object is soaked in alcohol acidified with oxalic acid and left for 1 day. The solutions are evaporated at 35 °C. 96% alcohol is added to the syrup to precipitate protein and foreign matter. It is then purified with ether 3 times. After that, in an alkaline medium, it is extracted with ether 3 more times.

t: History of the polar solvent methods
n: History of the polar solvent methods. The acidified alcohol method was improved by J.S. Stas in 1851 and F. Otto in 1856. The acidified water method was used by Z. Uslar and L. Erdmann in 1861. In 1942 Stepanov and Shvaykova, in 1946 Vasilyeva, and in 1956-1961 Kramarenko developed the methods further. That is, the methods were improved step by step by scientists of several generations.

Let us go through the Stas-Otto method step by step. The object is soaked several times in ethyl alcohol acidified with oxalic acid and left for 1 day. The alcoholic solutions are evaporated at 35 °C to a syrup; protein is precipitated with 96% alcohol. Warm water is added, and the mixture is purified with ether 3 times; the ether is discarded. The acidic solution is made alkaline with ammonia or sodium bicarbonate and extracted with ether 3 times. This extract contains the alkaloids.

Let us evaluate the Stas-Otto method. Disadvantages: it takes a long time, sensitivity is low, expensive alcohol is needed, and results vary. Advantage: substances can be isolated from a putrefied object; because purification is carried out in the presence of alcohol, an emulsion hardly forms. Later modifications concerned acidifying the object with various mineral acids and changing the alkalis and solvents.

Now let us compare the two methods. The Stas-Otto method takes a long time, has low sensitivity and needs expensive alcohol; but substances can be isolated from a putrefied object. The Vasilyeva method, on the other hand, is quick and does not need expensive reagents. However, with the Vasilyeva method it is difficult to isolate water-insoluble substances, and a stable emulsion forms in a putrefied object. This means that each of the two methods has its own advantages and disadvantages.

Acidified water methods. Evaluation: the method of M.D. Shvaykova and A.A. Vasilyeva is quick and does not need expensive reagents. Disadvantage: it is difficult to isolate water-insoluble substances, and complete isolation from a putrefied object is not possible. Historically, Uslar and Erdmann in 1861 acidified the object with HCl. Dragendorff used H2SO4 and extracted with 96% alcohol for 24 hours. Stepanov and Shvaykova in 1942 used oxalic acid-acidified water to isolate substances from plants. Vasilyeva in 1946 applied the method to cadaveric organs.

The Dragendorff method. The object is acidified with sulphuric acid, and the aqueous solution is evaporated to a syrup. It is then soaked for 24 hours in 96% alcohol and filtered; the filtrate is mixed with water. Acidic extraction is carried out with petrol, petroleum ether and chloroform, then the solution is made alkaline with ammonia and extracted with petrol and isoamyl alcohol. Disadvantage: heating the sulphuric acid extract leads to hydrolysis of ester-type alkaloids.

The principles of the Kramarenko method. V.F. Kramarenko, in 1956-1961, recommended taking into account the pH of the medium, the nature of the organic solvent and the effect of electrolytes, and using centrifugation instead of filtration. Alkaloids bind well to proteins in a weakly acidic medium, at pH 4-5. In a cadaver the pH is about 6.2, in a living organism 7.3-7.5. To break down complexes with protein, the pH must be brought to 2.5-3.

The pH values related to alkaloids and protein. Alkaloids bind well to proteins at pH 4-5. In a living organism the pH is 7.3-7.5, in a cadaver about 6.2. To break down protein complexes, a pH of 2.5-3 is reached. Thus the correct choice of pH determines the efficiency of isolation.

The acidic stage of the Kramarenko method. 100 g of the object is covered with 0.02 N H2SO4, brought to pH 2-2.5 with 20% H2SO4 and left for 2 hours. Soaking is repeated for a further 2 hours and 1 hour. The solutions are centrifuged and saturated with ammonium sulphate; after 1-2 hours the precipitate is separated. The centrifugate is extracted twice with 40 ml of ether. The ether is discarded or used for acidic substances.

The numbers of the Kramarenko method. 100 g of the object is taken. Sulphuric acid 0.02 N. The pH of the soaking medium is 2-2.5. The combined centrifugate is extracted twice with 40 ml of ether. 20% NaOH is added to the acidic solution to bring the pH to 8.5-9.0, and it is extracted with chloroform 3 times. Soaking lasts 2 hours, then a further 2 hours and 1 hour.

The alkaline stage of the Kramarenko method. 20% NaOH is added to the acidic solution to bring the pH to 8.5-9.0; ammonia is released and the pH changes. It is extracted with chloroform 3 times. The remaining layer is acidified and tested for iodide ion with NaNO2. If pachycarpine is present, the chloroform layer gives a red-pink colour.

t: Pachycarpine: scheme of the iodide ion reaction
n: The iodide ion reaction for pachycarpine. The alkaline aqueous layer remaining after extraction is acidified with acid. Sodium nitrite is added and the solution is tested for iodide ion; 1 ml of chloroform is added and shaken. If iodide ion is present, the chloroform layer forms a red-pink colour.

t: Current practice and the two isolates
n: Current practice and the two isolates. At present, on the basis of the Stas-Otto, Vasilyeva and Kramarenko methods, isolation is carried out with polar solvents at pH 2.5-3.0. Alkaloids are extracted from the aqueous isolate at pH 9; chloroform is the solvent most often used, sometimes ether. The two organic solutions obtained under acidic and alkaline conditions are analysed separately. In the acidic isolate, barbiturates, phenacetin, caffeine and strychnine are tested for. In the alkaline isolate, alkaloids and their synthetic analogues are tested for.

Liquid alkaloids. They include anabasine, nicotine, pachycarpine, coniine and arecoline. As bases they are oily liquids with a characteristic odour, fairly volatile and readily soluble in organic solvents. For this reason they are isolated by steam distillation under alkaline conditions. The distillate is made alkaline and extracted with chloroform.

t: Purification of the isolate: extraction and distillation
n: Purification of the isolate. Foreign substances interfere in the isolate, so the extracts are purified; there is no single exact method, and purification is based on physicochemical properties. Acidic substances, that is organic acids and barbiturates, are purified by re-extraction with alkali at pH 13 and acid at pH 1. Alkaloids are purified with acid at pH 1 and alkali at pH 13; weak bases, purine derivatives, narcotine, promedol, antipyrine and amidopyrine are lost. Dry distillation, that is sublimation, is used for sublimable substances such as barbiturates, benzoic and salicylic acids and caffeine.

t: Purification of the isolate: electrical and chromatographic methods
n: Electrical and chromatographic methods of purification. In electrodialysis, for strychnine and pachycarpine, alkaloid salts migrate towards the cathode under direct current. Electrophoresis is chromatographic purification under the action of current; the salts migrate towards the cathode at different rates. Chromatography, that is TLC, column gel and paper chromatography, gives an analysis of identity as well as purification from foreign substances.

Systems for chromatographic purification. For barbiturates: chloroform-n-butanol-25% NH4OH, in the ratio 70:40:5. Developing agent: 0.02% diphenylcarbazone in chloroform and mercury sulphate in dilute H2SO4. Barbiturates form ink-coloured spots, with different Rf values. For alkaloids: chloroform-acetone-diethylamine, 50:30:2, or chloroform-acetone-ammonia, 30:20:2. The developing agent is Dragendorff's reagent.

Rules for writing the report. The report is written on a single line of the notebook, with uniform spacing and no gaps, on both sides. A margin is left on the left of the first page and on the right of the second; unused lines are crossed out. Abbreviating words, using conventional symbols, writing authors' names against reagents and writing chemical formulae are prohibited. Corrections are marked in the margin with the words “the correction is to be trusted”, and the expert signs.

t: Structure of the report and the introductory part
n: Structure of the report. The report consists of three parts: introduction, description, and conclusion. The results are drawn up in the form of a “forensic chemical investigation report”. The introductory part is written without a heading: it states on the basis of which document, by whom, that is the student's full name, year, group, when and where the investigation was carried out, the physical evidence and the purpose. The introduction also gives the deceased's full name, the causes of death and a brief summary of the circumstances of the case.

Descriptive part. No heading is written in the descriptive part. First recorded are the external appearance of the biological object, its serial number, the pH of the medium, consistency and preservation. Second, the chemical investigation: the technique of isolating the poisons and the methods of determining the nature and quantity of the isolated substances are set out in detail, without abbreviation. In the chemical part of the report, the reagents and devices used and the calculations are given in sequence, based on the entries in the working notebook.

Concluding part. In the conclusion, on the basis of the investigation, the poisonous substances first detected and then not detected are written by name. The quantity of the poisons found is given in mg per 100 g of physical evidence; then the poisons for which a complete investigation gave a negative result are listed. The report is certified by the expert's signature and the time of writing is stated. When the quantity of ethyl alcohol is determined in blood and urine, the report is printed in two copies and certified with the expert chemist's seal.

t: Evaluating the result and storing the object
n: Evaluating the result and storing the object. The evaluation takes into account that the substance may have been eliminated before death, undergone metabolism, decomposed or combined with other substances. Because of the low sensitivity of the method, the substance may also fail to be detected. If a substance is detected, quantitative analysis must be carried out. A preserved object is kept for up to 1 year; objects containing alcohol are discarded after 1 month.

t: Storage periods for the object and documents
n: Storage periods. If the object is preserved, it is kept for up to 1 year. Documents are kept in a safe and discarded after 1 year. Objects containing alcohol are discarded after 1 month. Remember: for objects containing alcohol the period is the shortest.

t: Factors taken into account when evaluating the result
n: Factors taken into account when evaluating the result. The substance may be eliminated from the body before death or undergo metabolic changes. The substance may decompose entirely or combine with other substances. Because of the low sensitivity of the method, the substance may not be detected. Therefore a negative result does not always mean the absence of the substance.

Cases of false-positive reaction. When a substance is detected, quantitative analysis must always be carried out, because reactions characteristic of a harmless substance may sometimes appear. The victim may have taken the substance as a medicine. As a result of putrefaction of the object, compounds may form that give a reaction characteristic of the substance being sought. For this reason, a conclusion cannot be drawn relying on a qualitative reaction alone.

Case 14: red urine. Urine was brought to the forensic chemical examination as the biological object; the urine is red. Task: carry out the analysis and draw up a report. Case table: type of problem, causes of origin, ways of solution. For the analysis plan, an acidic and an alkaline isolate are obtained, and each is examined separately.

Conclusion. Organic poisons are isolated with polar solvents at pH 2.5-3.0; the acidic and alkaline isolates are analysed separately. The isolate is purified by re-extraction, dry distillation, electrodialysis, electrophoresis and chromatography. The report consists of three parts: introduction, description, conclusion. It contains no formulae or authors' names, and the conclusion lists the poisons found and not found by name.
